nodes.name: JPMorgan's suspicious-activity reports after the arrest (2019)
nodes.note: Filed with Treasury in 2019, six years after JPMorgan ended the relationship. USVI lawyers told the court in 2023 that they identified more than $1B in suspicious transactions. A SAR is a bank's alert, not a finding.

nodes.name: JPMorgan's transaction spreadsheet (2005-19)
nodes.note: Produced in the USVI case: more than 9,000 transactions to Epstein-related persons, 2005-2019, over $2.4B combined. The USVI says it shows more than $1.1M paid to "girls or women" after the bank cut him off, $320,000 of it to people with no earlier recorded payments, many with Eastern European surnames. JPMorgan denies wrongdoing.

nodes.name: Treasury records reviewed by Senate Finance staff (2024)
nodes.note: Viewed by committee staff at Treasury in 2024 and not released. Wyden: about 4,700 wire transfers at one bank, more than $1B in and out of one account; several Russian banks, now under sanctions, used for payments; many of the women and girls came from Russia, Belarus, Turkey and Turkmenistan. These are his descriptions of records the public has not seen.

nodes.name: Wyden's questions to JPMorgan (20 Oct 2025)
nodes.note: Senate Finance letter to Jamie Dimon: more than $1.7M in cash withdrawn from Epstein's accounts in 2004-05 (public reports); asks for transactions through correspondent accounts at Sberbank, Alfa Bank and FCB, and for named executives' records. Questions, not findings.

nodes.name: Sberbank
nodes.note: Russian state bank. Named in Wyden's Oct 2025 questions about correspondent-account transactions; no transaction has been published. Under US sanctions since 2022.

nodes.name: Alfa-Bank
nodes.note: Russian private bank. Named in the same questions; no transaction has been published. Under US sanctions since 2022.

nodes.name: William Langford
nodes.note: JPMorgan head of compliance. Reported to have urged, in 2010-11, a "rapid response" review of whether to exit Epstein (Wyden's letter, citing reporting).

nodes.name: Justin Nelson
nodes.note: JPMorgan banker named in Wyden's questions about the management of Epstein's accounts and 2013 memos.

nodes.name: HSBC France (Paris branch)
nodes.note: Ended Epstein's Paris account by letter a few days before Christmas 2007, with a month's notice. Bloomberg's sources say compliance had flagged payments linked to young women tied to Brunel's agency, round-dollar deposits and withdrawals. HSBC declined to comment.

nodes.name: BNP Paribas
nodes.note: Held an Epstein current account, savings and card, inherited from Fortis, from Feb 2008 to mid-2018 (Le Monde, 21 Feb 2026). What it was used for is not known.

nodes.name: Julius Baer
nodes.note: Swiss private bank. In spring 2017 its chief executive Boris Collardi and finance chief Dieter Enkelmann corresponded with Epstein about working with or buying Edmond de Rothschild; nothing came of it (finews.ch, from the Jan 2026 release).

nodes.name: Boris Collardi
nodes.note: Julius Baer chief executive to 2017. Met and corresponded with Epstein about Edmond de Rothschild in 2017; says the contact was professional.

nodes.name: Wexner-linked charitable fund (Jan 2008 transfer)
nodes.note: Received $46M from Epstein in January 2008 (tax records). Wexner's 2019 letter called it a "portion" of the money Epstein had misappropriated.

node_notes.nysdfs: New York regulator. $150M consent order against Deutsche Bank, 7 Jul 2020: hundreds of Epstein transactions totalling millions that should have drawn scrutiny, including settlement payments over $7M, more than $6M to law firms, payments to Russian models, tuition, hotel and rent for women, payments to numerous women with Eastern European surnames, payments to people alleged to have helped him, and cash withdrawals over $800,000 across about four years. Conditions set by a risk committee were not passed on or were misread.
